c10_bio_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c10_bio_ch01.scenario: At kilometre 30 of a marathon, a runner 'hits the wall': pace collapses, legs feel heavy, and his blood shows high lactate with depleted glucose. His friend shouts to just breathe harder and push through.
c10_bio_ch01.prompt: What actually explains the crash — and what helps?

options.text: His muscle glycogen is exhausted, so cells lean on anaerobic glycolysis; lactate and H+ build up, inhibiting the enzymes and contraction. Easing pace and taking carbs helps — faster breathing can't instantly raise oxygen delivery or clear lactate.
options.outcome: Recovery takes time: lactate must be oxidised in the muscle or shipped to the liver, and oxygen supply is limited by cardiac output, not just how fast he breathes.

options.text: The muscles ran out of oxygen, so breathing as fast as possible will immediately convert the lactate back into energy.
options.outcome: Oxygen delivery is capped by cardiac output and capillary diffusion; lactate still has to be cleared biochemically, which takes minutes, not a breath.

options.text: It's simple dehydration — a glass of water and he can sprint again.
options.outcome: Water helps hydration but doesn't restore glycogen or remove the acidosis blocking contraction.

c10_bio_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c10_bio_ch02.scenario: A wheat farmer's field is overrun with broadleaf weeds. The agri-store sells 2,4-D, a synthetic auxin. Wheat is a monocot; the weeds are dicots.
c10_bio_ch02.prompt: Will spraying 2,4-D clear the weeds without hurting the wheat?

options.text: Yes — 2,4-D mimics auxin, and dicots are far more sensitive to it: the overdose triggers uncontrolled, lethal growth in the weeds while the wheat tolerates or breaks it down.
options.outcome: Selective herbicide action: the same hormone-mimic exploits the difference in sensitivity between dicots and monocots.

options.text: No — any plant hormone will boost all plants equally, so it will just feed the weeds.
options.outcome: Sensitivity differs hugely by plant group; dicots are killed by auxin overload at doses monocots shrug off.

options.text: Use cytokinin instead — encouraging cell division will make the wheat outgrow the weeds.
options.outcome: Cytokinin doesn't kill weeds; competition alone won't clear an established weed infestation.

c10_bio_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c10_bio_ch03.scenario: In a seed lab, a trainee sorts seeds by the rule 'monocots keep endosperm, dicots never have it.' A castor seed — a dicot full of endosperm — lands on her bench and doesn't fit the rule.

options.text: By whether the endosperm survives into the mature seed, not by monocot vs dicot: castor keeps its endosperm (albuminous), while pea and bean absorb theirs into the cotyledons.
options.outcome: Both monocots and dicots come in albuminous and exalbuminous types — it's about seed development, not taxonomy.

options.text: Castor must be mislabelled — all dicots absorb their endosperm.
options.outcome: Castor and coconut are textbook dicots/monocots with persistent endosperm; the mature seed tells the truth, not the group name.

options.text: Cut the seed open; whichever side has more starch is a monocot.
options.outcome: Endosperm persistence is a developmental trait — the scutellum in maize or castor's endosperm don't change the plant's class.

c10_bio_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c10_bio_ch04.scenario: Birds keep eating the brightest fish in a pond. A classmate concludes: 'The fish will evolve duller colours because they need to hide from the birds.'
c10_bio_ch04.prompt: What's the right way to explain what will actually happen?

options.text: Colour variation already exists at random; birds simply eat bright fish more often, so dull fish survive and breed more — dull colour spreads over generations.
options.outcome: Natural selection works on existing heritable variation; the population changes because of who survives, not because anyone 'needs' to change.

options.text: She's right — facing predators pushes fish to produce duller offspring on purpose.
options.outcome: Mutations aren't aimed at a goal; predation only selects among variants that already exist.

options.text: Each bright fish will gradually darken its own scales to match the pond bottom.
options.outcome: An acquired colour change isn't written into the genes, so it wouldn't shift the population's colours over generations.

c10_chem_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c10_chem_ch01.scenario: In a metal-extraction demo, coke reduces iron oxide: 2Fe2O3 + 3C → 4Fe + 3CO2. A junior technician logs 'carbon is reduced, since it gains oxygen to become CO2.'

options.text: No — carbon gains oxygen and loses electrons, so it is oxidised and acts as the reducing agent; Fe2O3 loses oxygen and is reduced, making it the oxidising agent.
options.outcome: Gaining oxygen is oxidation by the classical definition, and electron loss confirms it — the carbon does the reducing.

options.text: Yes — 'gains oxygen' sounds like a gain, and gain means reduction.
options.outcome: Reduction is gain of electrons (or loss of oxygen); gaining oxygen is the opposite — oxidation.

options.text: Both are right — carbon is oxidised and reduced at the same time.
options.outcome: A species can't be both here; C goes to CO2 (oxidation) while Fe3+ goes to Fe (reduction).

c10_chem_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c10_chem_ch02.scenario: A quality-control lab receives an unlabelled white powder. It dissolves cleanly in dilute hydrochloric acid with no gas, and it also reacts with hot sodium hydroxide solution.
c10_chem_ch02.prompt: What kind of substance is it?

options.text: An amphoteric oxide such as zinc oxide — it behaves as a base toward the acid and as an acid toward the alkali because it sits between metallic and non-metallic character.
options.outcome: Amphoteric oxides like ZnO and Al2O3 neutralise both HCl and NaOH, e.g. ZnO + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2O and ZnO + 2NaOH → Na2ZnO2 + H2O.

options.text: A neutral salt — it dissolves in both, so it must be inert to both.
options.outcome: It isn't merely dissolving; it chemically neutralises each — a neutral salt wouldn't react with NaOH at all.

options.text: A strong base, because anything that reacts with acid is a base.
options.outcome: The reaction with NaOH rules that out — strong bases don't also neutralise bases.

c10_chem_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c10_chem_ch03.scenario: A recycler wants to cut costs on an aluminium plant. He proposes skipping the expensive electrolysis and just heating alumina (Al2O3) with coke, the way iron is won from haematite in a blast furnace.
c10_chem_ch03.prompt: Will the coke trick work for aluminium?

options.text: No — aluminium sits above carbon in the reactivity series, so carbon can't pull oxygen away from Al2O3; only electrolysis supplies enough energy to reduce it.
options.outcome: Carbon reduces only the oxides of metals below it — that works for iron but fails for aluminium, which is why Hall-Heroult electrolysis exists.

options.text: Yes — a hotter furnace and more coke can reduce any oxide.
options.outcome: Temperature isn't the deciding factor; the reactivity series is. Carbon simply can't displace a metal more reactive than itself.

options.text: Yes — iron and aluminium are extracted identically in industry anyway.
options.outcome: They aren't: iron uses carbon reduction in a blast furnace, aluminium uses electrolysis precisely because carbon can't do the job.

c10_chem_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c10_chem_ch04.scenario: Three unlabelled hydrocarbon fuels arrive at a lab. A technician adds orange bromine water to each: samples B and C turn colourless, sample A stays orange.
c10_chem_ch04.prompt: What has she learned about sample A?

options.text: A is a saturated hydrocarbon — an alkane with only single bonds, so there is no double or triple bond for bromine to add across; B and C are unsaturated.
options.outcome: Decolourising bromine water is the classic test for C=C or C≡C bonds; alkanes only substitute (slowly, in light) and leave the colour intact.

options.text: A failed the test, so it isn't a hydrocarbon at all.
options.outcome: Alkanes are hydrocarbons too — they just lack the pi bonds that decolourise bromine.

options.text: A is the most reactive — it didn't waste time reacting with bromine.
options.outcome: No colour change means no addition happened; unsaturation, not inertness, is what reacts fast with bromine.

c10_chem_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c10_chem_ch05.scenario: Reading the periodic table, a student predicts calcium (Group 2, Period 4) will react more gently with water than magnesium (Group 2, Period 3): 'It's heavier, so its electrons are held tighter.'

options.text: No — ionisation energy falls down the group because extra shells shield the outer electrons, so calcium lets go of them more easily and reacts more vigorously with water.
options.outcome: Ca + 2H2O → Ca(OH)2 + H2 is livelier than magnesium's slow reaction — reactivity rises down Group 2.

options.text: Yes — higher atomic number always means stronger hold on electrons.
options.outcome: Atomic number rises, but so do shells and shielding; down a group the outer electrons are actually lost more easily.

options.text: Neither — all Group 2 metals react with water at the same rate.
options.outcome: The trend is real and visible: Mg barely reacts with cold water while Ca bubbles steadily.

c10_eco_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c10_eco_ch01.scenario: A newspaper reports that State X has higher per-capita income than State Y, yet a larger share of underweight children. A columnist concludes: 'Income growth does nothing for nutrition.'
c10_eco_ch01.prompt: What's the strongest reading of the data?

options.text: Income is only an average — if growth is unequally shared or sanitation is poor, children stay underweight despite rising income; check long-term indicators like stunting rates before judging.
options.outcome: Development is multi-dimensional: health outcomes depend on distribution, public services and absorption of nutrients, not the average wallet.

options.text: The data must be wrong — higher income always means better-nourished children.
options.outcome: Per-capita income can rise while poor households and sanitation lag; the paradox is real, not a data error.

options.text: Income is meaningless — only calorie counts matter for development.
options.outcome: Income still matters; the point is it doesn't capture health, education or equity on its own.

c10_eco_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c10_eco_ch02.scenario: A district report shows MGNREGA households averaged about 50 days of work against the 100-day guarantee, women did over half the person-days, and states still owe thousands of crores in pending wages. An official says the shortfall proves villagers don't want the work.
c10_eco_ch02.prompt: How should the 50-day figure be read?

options.text: Households mainly need fallback work in the lean season — roughly 50-60 days — and rising non-farm wages pull some away; the real failure to chase is the wage backlog, which violates the 15-day payment rule.
options.outcome: Low average take-up reflects when the work is needed, not the scheme's worth; unpaid wages are the actionable violation.

options.text: Fifty days means the guarantee is pointless and the scheme should be scrapped.
options.outcome: A guarantee is a safety net — people use what they need; lean-season demand explains the average without making it useless.

options.text: It proves households prefer leisure to guaranteed wages.
options.outcome: The demand is seasonal and wage-delayed; laziness doesn't explain women supplying 54% of the person-days.

c10_eco_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c10_eco_ch03.scenario: A women's self-help group has built a corpus of several lakh rupees through monthly savings and internal lending at 2% a month. A bank offers them a low-interest loan; the village moneylender offers a bigger sum instantly at 3% a month.
c10_eco_ch03.prompt: Which door should they knock on?

options.text: The bank — the SHG's joint liability and peer pressure work as 'social collateral,' which is exactly what unlocks cheap formal credit for people with no property to pledge.
options.outcome: Repayment discipline is enforced socially, so the bank can lend at rates the moneylender's 3%-a-month compounding can't match.

options.text: The moneylender — more money, faster, no paperwork.
options.outcome: Speed is the trap: monthly rates compound brutally and informal loans carry no consumer protection, which is how debt spirals start.

options.text: Neither — groups that lend to each other should never borrow outside.
options.outcome: Bank linkage is how SHGs scale up; refusing formal credit wastes the social collateral they've already built.

c10_eco_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c10_eco_ch04.scenario: A small powerloom owner buys yarn at market price and sells grey cloth locally. Since cheap imports surged, his profits have collapsed. A buyer suggests he 'just export directly — globalisation is a free market.'

options.text: Pool with other small units — a cluster or cooperative can share certification, marketing and larger orders, spreading the fixed costs a single small loom can't carry.
options.outcome: Export compliance and small order sizes are scale problems; collective organisation gives small producers the economies of scale a composite mill gets internally.

options.text: Export alone anyway — globalisation means anyone can sell anywhere.
options.outcome: Market access isn't free: quality certification and minimum order sizes are fixed costs that crush a 20-loom unit.

options.text: Lobby for a total ban on imports — that's the only way small producers survive.
options.outcome: Protectionism ignores the real gap — scale and compliance capacity — and closed markets carry their own costs for consumers and competitiveness.

c10_eco_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c10_eco_ch05.scenario: A shopper pays Rs 450 for a 1-litre bottle of 'virgin coconut oil' bearing an FSSAI licence number and an Agmark logo. At home the oil solidifies at 28°C though pure coconut oil sets near 24°C, and the bottle holds only 880 g against the labelled 910 g.

options.text: Keep the bottle, bill and photos as evidence, get a lab test if needed, and file a complaint — the raised solidification point signals adulteration and the weight gap is under-weighing, regardless of the logos.
options.outcome: A licence number shows registration, not purity; evidence plus the consumer forum is the working remedy.

options.text: Nothing — an FSSAI licence and Agmark on the label guarantee the oil is pure.
options.outcome: Logos can be printed or faked; the physical evidence (solidification point, short weight) overrides the label.

options.text: Just leave a bad review online — reviews are the modern consumer court.
options.outcome: A review warns others but recovers nothing; adulteration and short weight are legal violations the forum can actually redress.

c10_math_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch01.scenario: Marking a friend's proof that root-3 is irrational, you read: 'a squared equals 3b squared, so a is a multiple of 3.' The teacher docked a mark at exactly that line.

options.text: The justification: since 3 is prime and divides a squared, the prime-factor theorem forces 3 to divide a — and the same theorem is needed later for b.
options.outcome: The proof's engine is 'if a prime divides a square, it divides the number'; stating it makes the contradiction airtight.

options.text: Nothing — a square being a multiple of 3 obviously means the number is too.
options.outcome: 'Obviously' is the skipped step; without the prime theorem the argument has a hole a marker must dock.

options.text: She should have started by assuming root-3 is rational — that's the missing line.
options.outcome: She did assume it via 'root-3 = a/b'; the gap is the divisibility theorem, not the setup.

c10_math_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch02.scenario: A friend coding a polynomial-divider app claims a shortcut: 'If p(x) divided by (x-a)(x-b) leaves remainder R(x), then the remainder on dividing by (x-a) alone is just R(a).'
c10_math_ch02.prompt: Should the app use the shortcut?

options.text: Yes — since p(x) = (x-a)(x-b)Q(x) + R(x), plugging in x = a kills the divisor term, so p(a) = R(a); by the remainder theorem that is the remainder for division by (x-a).
options.outcome: The remainder theorem turns evaluation into remainder-reading — the shortcut is a theorem, not a hack.

options.text: No — every new divisor needs a fresh long division; remainders don't transfer.
options.outcome: They do: evaluating at the root of any factor collapses p to R there, which is exactly what the remainder theorem uses.

options.text: Only if R(x) is a constant — a linear remainder breaks it.
options.outcome: Degree doesn't matter; p(a) = R(a) holds whatever R looks like, because the (x-a) factor still vanishes at x = a.

c10_math_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch03.scenario: Solving for fruit prices, a student hits 3x + 2y = 12 and 6x + 4y = 24. Cross-multiplication gives x/0 = y/0 = 1/0, and he writes 'x = y = 0, unique solution.'

options.text: The two equations are the same straight line — every point on it is a solution, so there are infinitely many; 0/0 is undefined, not zero.
options.outcome: When all ratios coincide the equations are dependent (coincident lines); the vanishing denominators are the signal of infinite solutions.

options.text: Zero over zero equals zero, so his x = y = 0 stands.
options.outcome: 0/0 is indeterminate — and (0,0) doesn't even satisfy the equations, since 0 + 0 isn't 12.

options.text: A zero denominator proves the equations have no solution at all.
options.outcome: No-solution happens when the sides are proportional but the constants aren't (parallel lines); here constants match too, giving infinitely many solutions.

c10_math_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch04.scenario: A boat runs at 15 km/h in still water. It goes 30 km upstream and returns in 4.5 hours total. A trainee says 'the stream could be any speed — the equation will sort it out.'
c10_math_ch04.prompt: Does a real stream speed exist?

options.text: Yes — the timings reduce to x squared = 25 with discriminant 100 > 0, giving x = 5 km/h; the negative root is physically meaningless, not a second answer.
options.outcome: A positive discriminant guarantees real roots; the upstream/downstream model then selects the positive one as the actual stream speed.

options.text: Two real roots mean two valid stream speeds: +5 and -5 km/h.
options.outcome: Speed can't be negative; the minus root is an algebraic leftover, not a physical option.

options.text: No — since time is fixed, any equation for the stream must be contradictory.
options.outcome: The equation is perfectly consistent; checking the discriminant before solving shows a real positive speed exists.

c10_math_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch05.scenario: A savings app shows total savings after n weeks follows S(n) = 3n squared + 5n (in tens of rupees). The product team asks: 'What's the weekly deposit pattern, and what's the week-15 deposit?'
c10_math_ch05.prompt: How do you recover the AP?

options.text: First term a = S(1) = 8, and the common difference is twice the n-squared coefficient, so d = 6; the 15th deposit is a + 14d = 92 (i.e. Rs 920).
options.outcome: For S(n) = An squared + Bn, the underlying AP always has a = A + B and d = 2A — the quadratic coefficient is half the difference.

options.text: The first deposit is 3 — the coefficient of n squared is the starting term.
options.outcome: That coefficient is half the common difference (d = 2A); the first term is S(1) = 3 + 5 = 8.

options.text: Deposit amounts can't be recovered from a total — you'd need the app data.
options.outcome: S(n) encodes everything: S(1) gives a, and a(n) = S(n) - S(n-1) gives every term.

c10_math_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch06.scenario: An architect's roof truss has sides 6 m and 8 m meeting at 60°. A modelmaker builds a scale version with 15 cm and 20 cm sides, also at 60°, and a checker asks: 'Prove the model is similar — did you measure the third side?'
c10_math_ch06.prompt: Is the similarity proven without the third side?

options.text: Yes — the included angle matches and the flanking sides share one ratio (600/15 = 800/20 = 40), so SAS similarity holds; every length just scales by 40.
options.outcome: SAS similarity needs two proportional sides plus the equal included angle — the third side then follows automatically at the same scale.

options.text: No — similarity requires all three sides measured and compared.
options.outcome: SSS is only one route; SAS and AA each prove similarity without touching the third side.

options.text: No — the units differ (metres vs centimetres), so the triangles can't be similar.
options.outcome: Similarity is about ratios, not units; converting to the same unit is exactly what reveals the common factor of 40.
